purpose: Map the high-density biblical chain around women mourning a dead/disappeared male figure, gates, tombs, removed stones, absent bodies, return, and gardener imagery, then compare those motifs to the Tim Dooley Son/Thomas archive without treating resemblance as prediction or proof.
method_rules: Project-side event first; biblical comparator second.
Keep direct textual overlap distinct from later symbolic synthesis.
Do not identify modern people with biblical figures merely because roles overlap.
Do not repeat the traditional but textually unsupported claim that Mary Magdalene was a prostitute; the New Testament does not call her one.
For Sammy, preserve 'lady of the night' only as the user's characterization unless independently documented.

core_chain.boundary: Ezekiel portrays a condemned cultic scene; it is not a prediction of a modern event.

core_chain.strength: very high structural comparator because gate + woman + dead son + weeping + restoration occur in one short sequence

core_chain.note: This is the strongest single Christian tomb comparator currently found because the sequence bundles darkness + woman + tomb + removed stone + absence + tears + gardener + return + Father.

core_chain.boundary: Thomas is not Lazarus in the text; this is adjacency and motif chaining, not identity.

socially_marginal_women_comparators.biblical_status: explicitly called a prostitute in Joshua; later appears in Matthew's genealogy leading to David/Jesus
socially_marginal_women_comparators.project_use: Possible comparator to the user's description of Sammy as a 'lady of the night': marginal social status does not exclude witness, agency or theological importance.
socially_marginal_women_comparators.boundary: No claim that Sammy is Rahab.

socially_marginal_women_comparators.biblical_status: a widow who disguises herself so Judah thinks she is a prostitute; later included in Jesus' genealogy
socially_marginal_women_comparators.project_use: Useful only as a role comparator for stigma, sexuality, boundary/gateway imagery and later theological inclusion.
socially_marginal_women_comparators.boundary: Tamar is not straightforwardly a sex worker identity; she uses a disguise within a specific family/legal crisis.

socially_marginal_women_comparators.biblical_status: disciple/witness at the tomb; not called a prostitute in the New Testament
socially_marginal_women_comparators.project_use: The strongest comparison is mourning-witness function, not sexual status.

new_relational_findings.finding: Ezekiel 8 and Luke 7 create a notable two-gate structure: at one gate women mourn Tammuz; at another gate a woman mourns her dead only son, who is then raised. The project independently carries North Gate + woman mourning Thomas/Tammuz + Son-return language.

John 20 places a mourning woman at an emptied tomb, then has her mistake the returned Jesus for the gardener before Jesus speaks of ascending to the Father. This creates a later textual chain Tomb → Woman/Weeping → Missing Body → Gardener → Recognition → Father that strongly overlaps project vocabulary while remaining a comparison rather than identity claim.

The project still lacks a securely recovered contemporary 'rolled stone' statement, but John 20 supplies the biblical stone-removal side exactly. Therefore stone should remain 'biblical-side confirmed / project-side unresolved' until a dated Tim/Son source is recovered.

Across Luke 7, Luke 23, John 20 and Ezekiel 8, women are not incidental scenery: their mourning marks death, loss, boundary crossing, recognition or restoration. This makes Sammy's role as a mourning commenter structurally more relevant than treating her only as a peripheral character.

Rahab and Tamar show that socially stigmatized or sexually marginal female figures can occupy decisive positions in biblical narrative and even genealogy. This supports a broad cultural comparator for Sammy's user-described social role, but not a one-to-one biblical identity.
